papers.what_it_is: A quantum-chemistry methods paper that rewrites Hartree-Fock-style SCF as a sequence of QUSO/QUBO/MaxCut problems, derives a per-step approximation guarantee from semidefinite programming, tests it classically on the hydroxide anion and N2 dissociation, and outlines four hybrid quantum-classical variants (GAS, QAOA, QA, DQI) that it does not run.

existing.note: The body limits the guarantee: it bounds only the single Slater determinant (1-RDM) chosen in the current MO basis at each step, as a fraction of optimal set by the approximation algorithm; the SCF MaxCut graphs have negative edge weights, so the 0.878 Goemans-Williamson ratio does not apply directly and the derived bound is problem-dependent and likely loose; it does not hold for multi-reference methods such as CASSCF.
existing.value: The authors state that applying semidefinite programming to the MaxCut-SCF problem ensures, at each step, that the single Slater determinant (1-RDM) chosen in the current molecular orbital basis is within a fraction of optimal determined by the approximation algorithm, a guarantee absent from conventional Hartree-Fock. Because the MaxCut graph can have negative edge weights, the bound is problem-dependent: the Goemans-Williamson ratio of 0.878 holds for positive weights only, and their bound with negative weights (Equation F8) is likely loose. The analysis does not hold for multi-reference SCF methods such as CASSCF.

papers.what_it_is: A theory paper that defines when a quantum classifier is single-shot (near-deterministic from one run), lower-bounds the single-shot error by quantum multi-hypothesis testing of the embedded states, turns that into circuit-depth requirements for noiseless and depolarized embeddings, and argues that generically single-shot models generalize poorly.

existing.note: Section V is an argument, not a theorem: it covers 'generically accurate' single-shot models (an accurate single-shot POVM exists for every labeling), assumes all data points are at least ξ apart, treats binary classification, and rests on a cited sample-complexity bound for learning a POVM effect.
existing.value: The authors argue, not as a stated theorem, that a generically accurate single-shot model (one for which an accurate single-shot POVM exists for every possible labeling) cannot generalize well: assuming all data points are at least ξ apart and considering binary classification, such a model must map separated inputs to nearly orthogonal directions, so the Hilbert-space dimension, and by a cited bound the number of training samples needed to learn the POVM, grows like the number of ξ-balls covering the input space, which is inefficient in the input size.

existing.note: Adds the two theorem statements and their conditions. The Bayesian bound (Theorem 6) is the optimal multi-hypothesis error for the average states of the classes the classifier itself assigns; the depth bound (Theorem 9) holds for an L-layer circuit encoding each feature once per layer, and gives the needed depth as inversely proportional to the average inter-class distance.
existing.value: The paper proves that if a classifier has the Bayesian single-shot property, its single-shot error δ is at least the optimal Bayesian multi-hypothesis testing error between the average embedded states of the classes the classifier itself assigns. For an embedding by a noiseless parametrized circuit of L layers that encodes each data feature once per layer, it proves the single-shot error is bounded by the worst average distance between two data classes, so either the classes are far apart in input space or the circuit is sufficiently deep; with equally likely classes the required number of layers is inversely proportional to the average distance between classes. The authors note the bound need not be achieved by the circuit.

assertions.value: The authors show that the Hilbert-Schmidt test cost is bounded by the Frobenius-norm cost, so minimizing the Frobenius cost automatically minimizes the Hilbert-Schmidt cost.

assertions.value: The authors state that although a classical implementation computes gradients directly, so an exponentially small gradient is in principle less serious than when it must be estimated by measurement, in practice barren plateaus still raise training times beyond practical limits and appear even with small numbers of qubits.
